title: Working with Purpose, on Purpose
hook: Eleven Miles Davis words turned purpose from a poster into a working tool.
counterintuition: A noble mission does not live in a statement. It lives in what the team repeats when the room is busy.
tryThisNow: Choose one value and ask where it should show up in today's work before anyone gets tired.
keyTakeaway: Purpose gets practical when values move from posters into decisions, language, and the daily rhythm of the team.

breakdown.fastRead: An early review said the dining room needed a bit of Miles Davis, more reinvention, more forward motion. The team could have shrugged it off as a slight. Instead they studied the musician, pulled out the words people used to describe him, and hung eleven of them in the kitchen where everyone would see them every shift. A vague aspiration became a daily measuring stick. That is the work. Purpose does not arrive on its own. It gets engineered, named, written down, and repeated, until it shapes what the team actually does.
breakdown.deepRead: Why post eleven adjectives on a kitchen wall? A vision means nothing until it is concrete and visible enough to measure a choice against. Cool, fresh, spontaneous, adventurous, endless reinvention: the words were lifted from descriptions of Miles Davis and turned into a working roadmap the team could check itself against on a busy night. The same instinct drove a bigger exercise. Roughly a hundred and fifty people spent a full day distilling the whole operation down to four non-negotiable values: education, passion, excellence, and hospitality. Two of them, excellence and hospitality, were deliberately left in tension, because forcing two competing standards to coexist demands constant invention instead of an easy compromise. None of this was branding. The point was to give people a shared why they could act on, and a common language for it, so that when the room got loud the values were not a poster but the thing the team reached for. Two values in tension force a real choice every shift, and that friction is where the invention happens.
breakdown.fullRead: Purpose is not a soft byproduct that appears when morale is high. It is a deliberate construction project, and the most common way it fails is the easy one: a leader treats it as branding, posts a statement, and changes nothing about how decisions get made. Manufacturing real purpose means naming the values out loud, writing them where people see them, repeating the message, and refusing to dodge the hard tensions between them. Part of that construction is reframing the work itself. Serving others, through the lens of hospitality, was cast openly as a noble pursuit, something to take pride in instead of apologizing for. That message gives people permission to feel the dignity in caring for strangers, and a team that believes its work matters performs at a level a team going through the motions never reaches. The dignity is not decoration. A crew that sees its work as noble holds a higher bar for itself and stays when the work gets hard, because people pour themselves into something that means something and coast through something that does not. A sharp distinction sits underneath it. Service is what you do, the technical act of delivering something well. Hospitality is how that delivery makes a person feel. Keeping the two separate is what keeps purpose from collapsing into mere efficiency, because a team can execute flawlessly and still leave people cold if it forgets the second half. That is why the two values were held in tension on purpose. Drop hospitality and you get cold precision; drop excellence and you get warm sloppiness; keep both and you are forced to keep inventing. None of this is restaurant-only. Any organization can mine an outside critique for an identity, name a few values together, post them where choices get measured, and say plainly that the work is worth pride. A warehouse team, a support desk, a school faculty, each can take an outside critique, distill a few words it wants to be known for, and post them where the daily choices actually get made. The limit keeps it honest. Purpose is not a slogan or a one-day offsite that everyone forgets by Monday. It is values turned into daily decisions and shared language. The honest test is whether a normal team can point to a recent choice the values actually changed, not just a statement on the wall. When it can, purpose has stopped being branding and become the standard the team measures itself against.

examples.title: Wave off the critique or mine it

planSpec.stakes: A throwaway line in an early review of EMP,that the dining room needed a bit of Miles Davis,became the seed of an entire creative identity once the team chose to take it seriously
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: A sharp critic says Augustin Moreau's design studio is technically perfect but lifeless, missing any spirit of Miles Davis. Augustin, the studio's creative director, can bristle and dismiss the jab, or do what the Eleven Madison Park team did: take the metaphor seriously and mine it for an identity. The studio wants him to laugh it off. Minutes before the staff meeting begins, Augustin is about to decide whether to wave away the critique or turn it into the north star his team has been missing.
examples.whatToDo: Treat a stinging outside critique as raw material for identity in place of an insult, mining the metaphor for a concrete north star your team can actually aim at.
examples.whyItMatters: People perform extraordinarily when they understand what they are reaching for and believe it is worth reaching for. Manufacturing that clarity and dignity intentionally is what separates a group that merely executes tasks from one capable of becoming the best in the world.

examples.title: Values only in your head

planSpec.stakes: Studying the qualities used to describe Miles Davis produced a list of eleven words,cool, endless reinvention, inspired, forward moving, fresh, collaborative, spontaneous, vibrant,
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: 'We have great values, everyone knows them,' the founder said. Bianca Sorrentino, the culture director, was not convinced. 'If they live only in your head, they do nothing. Eleven Madison Park hung eleven words in the kitchen so every choice could be measured against them.' She uncapped a marker. 'Before the offsite ends, you have to decide which few words go on the wall where the team actually sees them every day.'
examples.whatToDo: Make your values physical and visible where the team sees them daily, because a vision that lives only in someone's head cannot guide a single concrete choice.
examples.whyItMatters: Purpose is not a soft, feel-good byproduct that shows up if morale is high,it is a deliberate construction project. You manufacture it on purpose by naming values, writing them down where people see them, and refusing the easy path of choosing only one of two conflicting standards. And the uncomfortable claim underneath it all: service is not beneath anyone; treating it as menial is the actual failure of imagination.

examples.title: Harmony or productive friction

planSpec.stakes: A vision means nothing until it is made concrete and visible; turning an abstract aspiration into a posted vocabulary lets everyone measure their daily choices against it.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: Kwame Osei's team drafted a list of twelve nice-sounding values, and now the team lead must cut it down. The safe path keeps only values that agree with each other. The harder path keeps two that openly conflict, like excellence and hospitality, because forcing them to coexist drives real innovation, a tension Eleven Madison Park kept alive on purpose. The team wants comfort. Before the values are ratified Friday, Kwame has to choose harmony or productive friction.
examples.whatToDo: Pick a small set of values together and keep two that genuinely conflict, because forcing competing standards to coexist drives constant innovation instead of an easy, lifeless compromise.
examples.whyItMatters: A vision means nothing until it is made concrete and visible; turning an abstract aspiration into a posted vocabulary lets everyone measure their daily choices against it.

examples.title: Naming the work as noble

planSpec.stakes: An all-staff effort,roughly 150 people working through a full day,distilled the operation down to four non-negotiable core values: education, passion, excellence, and hospitality.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: Before, Faye Lindgren's warehouse crew saw their jobs as invisible drudgery, and it showed in how they treated each other. After Faye, the site manager, started naming the work as genuinely noble, an idea Eleven Madison Park preached when it told staff that serving others is a pursuit worth real pride, something shifted. She said it out loud, often. A year later the crew carried themselves differently, because someone had finally given them permission to feel proud of the work.
examples.whatToDo: Say out loud that the work is noble and name who it cares for, because openly dignifying the work gives people permission to take pride in it instead of treating it as menial.
examples.whyItMatters: Purpose is created by openly dignifying the work, reframing how people see themselves and what they are capable of giving.

examples.title: Purpose treated as branding

planSpec.stakes: Excellence and hospitality were deliberately held in tension as competing goals, because forcing two seemingly conflicting standards to coexist drives constant innovation instead o
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: Engagement scores stayed flat, so the division director Rohan Mehta reviewed the year Monday. He had assumed purpose would simply emerge if he hired good people and kept morale up. Reading the survey, Rohan saw the error: he had treated purpose as a hope, or worse as branding, while daily choices stayed unchanged. Like the deliberate work at Eleven Madison Park, purpose is a construction project, manufactured by naming values, posting them, and refusing easy compromises, none of which he had actually done.
examples.whatToDo: Stop hoping purpose will emerge on its own and build it deliberately by naming values, making them visible, and changing daily choices, because purpose is a construction project, not a byproduct.
examples.whyItMatters: A noble mission does not live in a statement. It lives in what the team repeats when the room is busy.

examples.title: New clinic: task list or a why

planSpec.stakes: Service work carries genuine dignity and nobility, and naming that out loud gives people permission to feel pride in taking care of others instead of treating it as menial.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: Two weeks before the new clinic opens, the practice director Sigrid Holm must decide how to set the team's purpose. The easy plan lists tasks and protocols. The harder plan first names a shared why and the distinction between service, the technical act, and hospitality, how it makes a patient feel, a shared why Eleven Madison Park built deliberately. The board wants the task list. Sigrid weighs efficiency now against a team that knows what it is really for.
examples.whatToDo: Before listing tasks, give the team a shared why and the distinction between doing the work and how it makes people feel, because a named purpose is what aligns a team for greatness.
examples.whyItMatters: Purpose gets practical when values move from posters into decisions, language, and the daily rhythm of the team.

questions.prompt: A leader insists, 'If I hire good people and keep morale up, a sense of purpose will just emerge.' Engagement stays flat. What does this miss about purpose?
choices: Nothing; purpose reliably appears on its own wherever morale is high and the people are talented.
Purpose is built deliberately by naming values and making them visible, not a byproduct that emerges from good vibes.
Purpose is irrelevant to engagement, so the flat scores must come from something unrelated to meaning.
questions.explanation: Purpose is a deliberate construction project, not a feel-good byproduct. You build it by naming values, posting them where people see them, and refusing easy compromises, which high morale does not do on its own.

questions.prompt: When a stinging review calls a team technically flawless but lifeless, and the team wants to dismiss it, what is the more useful response?
choices: Take the metaphor seriously and mine it for a concrete identity the team can aim at, as opposed to brushing it off.
Reject it outright, since a harsh review rarely contains anything a strong team should act on.
Demand a retraction, because the only fix for a bad review is to discredit the critic who wrote it.
questions.explanation: An aspirational identity can be reverse-engineered from outside criticism. Taking the metaphor seriously and mining it for a north star turns a sting into direction, instead of wasted defensiveness.

questions.prompt: A founder says everyone already knows the company's values, though they live only in his head. Behavior is inconsistent. What should he do?
choices: Keep the values in his head, since writing them down would only make them feel rigid and corporate.
Make a few values physical and visible where the team sees them daily, so every choice can be measured against them.
Replace the values with detailed task rules, because concrete instructions matter more than any stated values.
questions.explanation: A vision means nothing until it is concrete and visible. Posting a short, shared vocabulary lets everyone measure daily choices against it, which values trapped in one head cannot do.

questions.prompt: While trimming a long values list, one instinct is to keep only values that agree with each other. Which approach better builds productive tension?
choices: Keep only harmonious values, since values that conflict will paralyze the team with constant arguments.
Keep all twelve values, because more stated values signal a richer, more thoughtful culture.
Keep two values that genuinely conflict, like excellence and hospitality, since forcing them to coexist drives real innovation.
questions.explanation: Holding two competing standards in tension drives constant innovation instead of easy compromise. Choosing values that genuinely conflict, not just agreeable ones, is what pushes a team to invent.

questions.prompt: A warehouse crew sees their jobs as invisible drudgery and treat each other carelessly. A manager wants to shift that. Which move best fits the idea of dignifying the work?
choices: Offer a small attendance bonus, since money is the only thing that changes how people view their jobs.
Tell them the work is humble and to simply accept it, because pretending it matters would feel dishonest.
Name the work as genuinely noble and tie it to the real people it serves, giving the crew permission to feel pride.
questions.explanation: Affirming the nobility of the work out loud reframes how people see themselves and gives them permission to take pride in caring for others, which a bonus or a shrug cannot do.

questions.prompt: A company plasters purpose statements everywhere, but daily decisions never change. Engagement does not move. What best diagnoses the problem?
choices: The statements are not displayed prominently enough, so the fix is simply bigger and bolder signage.
Engagement is random noise, so no purpose effort could plausibly move it in either direction.
Purpose was treated as branding while behavior stayed the same; it only works when it changes real daily choices.
questions.explanation: Purpose treated as branding, with unchanged daily choices, is the failure mode. It becomes real only when values actually govern decisions, not when they are merely posted as slogans.

questions.prompt: A new manager tells the team, 'Service and hospitality are the same thing done well, so if we execute cleanly we get both.' How should you evaluate that claim?
choices: Push back: service is the technical act of delivering something, while hospitality is how that delivery makes a person feel.
Agree, since well-executed service is the same as the feeling that defines hospitality.
Agree, because the difference between the two is purely academic and rarely affects real work.
questions.explanation: Service and hospitality are distinct: service is delivering the thing well, hospitality is how it makes the person feel. Collapsing them ignores the emotional layer that actually creates connection.

questions.prompt: You are starting a new team and want a shared why that guides behavior, not just a slogan. What is the strongest plan?
choices: Write an inspiring mission statement, frame it on the wall, and assume the words alone will shape behavior.
Define a small set of values together, post them visibly, and judge daily choices against them as a team.
Skip values and focus only on metrics, since numbers are the only purpose a team really needs.
questions.explanation: Manufacturing purpose means naming values collectively, making them visible, and measuring choices against them. A framed slogan or pure metrics cannot supply the shared why that guides behavior.

questions.prompt: Your team gets a harsh outside critique that stings but contains a real metaphor. You want to use it the way a purposeful leader would. What is the best move?
choices: Study the metaphor, pull a concrete vocabulary from it, and post that as a shared roadmap the team can aim at.
Bury the critique so it does not hurt morale, since dwelling on criticism only demoralizes a team.
Adopt the critic's exact words as your slogan without interpretation, because the critic clearly knows best.
questions.explanation: An identity can be reverse-engineered from a critique. Mining the metaphor for a concrete, posted vocabulary turns the sting into a usable north star, instead of hiding it or copying it blindly.

reviewCards.front: Beyond running things competently, what must a leader decide and change to give a team real purpose?
reviewCards.back: Decide to manufacture purpose deliberately by naming a small set of values, making them visible, and judging daily choices against them, instead of hoping meaning emerges on its own.

reviewCards.front: What does a technically perfect but lifeless operation reveal about what its standards are missing?
reviewCards.back: It reveals that competence without a shared why produces precision but no spirit; the missing standard is a deliberately built purpose, not more technical polish.

reviewCards.front: Why does manufacturing purpose on purpose transfer from a restaurant to any organization?
reviewCards.back: Because purpose is a construction project, not a feel-good byproduct; any team can reverse-engineer an identity, name its values, and post them where choices get measured.

reviewCards.front: What is the most common way leaders let purpose become branding while behavior stays the same?
reviewCards.back: They write an inspiring statement and post it everywhere, then change nothing about how decisions actually get made, so the values stay on the wall and never reach the daily work.

reviewCards.front: What single question helps a manager coach a team toward a shared, usable purpose?
reviewCards.back: Ask: 'What do we want to be known for, and is that value visible enough that we can measure today's choices against it?'

reviewCards.front: Purpose can be a poster slogan. What turns it into a standard a team measures choices against?
reviewCards.back: When the values are chosen together, including ones that productively conflict, posted where people see them, and actually used to make daily decisions.

implementationPlan.title: Working with Purpose, on Purpose Operating Habit
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Manufacture purpose on purpose: mine an outside critique or a metaphor for an identity, name a small set of values, including two that productively conflict, and post them where the team sees them daily. Say out loud that the work is noble, and judge choices against the values, because purpose is built deliberately, not hoped into being.

ifThenPlans.context: The team is technically excellent but feels lifeless, with no shared sense of why it exists.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the metric and the felt experience diverge, then investigate the feeling before defending the process.

ifThenPlans.context: A vivid metaphor for the team's identity becomes a slogan no one measures choices against.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the idea becomes a slogan, then translate it into a behavior with an owner and a deadline.

ifThenPlans.context: Purpose becomes a posted statement while the daily choices stay exactly the same.
ifThenPlans.plan: If drift appears, then restate the intended feeling and remove one barrier to acting on it.

ifThenPlans.context: Turning a harsh critique into a north star raises the ambition of the whole room.
ifThenPlans.plan: If ambition rises, then pair it with a simple inspection: did the receiver feel part of work that matters?

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Write down the one value you most want your team known for, then check three of today's decisions against it and rework any choice that does not match.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask the team for one example where the lesson changed a decision, not just a conversation.

memorableLines.why: It explains why values must be made physical.
